questions.question: SVG stands for:
questions.explanation: SVG is an XML-based vector format that scales without quality loss — resolution independent.

questions.question: A key advantage over <canvas> is SVG is:

options.text: Retained-mode (DOM nodes) — each shape is selectable, styleable, and accessible

questions.explanation: SVG elements are real DOM nodes (can be targeted by CSS/JS, given ARIA). Canvas is an opaque bitmap.

questions.question: An SVG drawn with <circle cx='50' cy='50' r='40'> places its center at:
questions.explanation: cx/cy are the center coordinates; r is the radius. SVG origin is top-left, y downward like canvas.

questions.question: SVG scales crisply because it is:

options.text: Vector math (paths/curves), not a fixed pixel grid

questions.explanation: Vectors are recalculated at any size, so no pixelation — ideal for logos and icons.

questions.question: You can style SVG via:

options.text: CSS (fill, stroke) and/or presentation attributes (fill=, stroke=)

questions.explanation: Both CSS properties and SVG attributes control fill/stroke; CSS classes let you theme icons easily.

questions.question: SVG vs an icon: inline SVG lets you:

options.text: Recolor/animate/manipulate it with CSS and JS at runtime

questions.explanation: Inlining SVG makes each path a DOM node — you can change fill on hover, animate paths, add a11y. is opaque.

questions.question: For accessibility, an inline SVG icon should usually have:
questions.explanation: Meaningful icons need an accessible name; purely decorative ones should be aria-hidden to avoid noise.

questions.question: A common use case best suited to SVG is:

options.text: Logos, icons, and diagrams that must stay sharp at any size

questions.explanation: SVG excels at sharp, small, animatable vector art; use canvas/raster for photos and heavy pixel work.
